Welcome to NEXUS AI, an AI-powered platform for reporting civic problems and following them through to resolution. The promise on this title slide is: report, detect, resolve, and transform communities.

This slide is the civic infrastructure gap. Roads, drains, garbage, and street lights fail in the real world. On the system side, paper files move between departments, get delayed or lost, and often remain unresolved because the responsible office is unclear.

The NEXUS AI ecosystem sits between three roles. A citizen reports from a phone. The engine uses the photo and the location to route the case. An official desk tracks the resolution. The comparison below replaces manual entry and guesswork with mobile reporting, boundary-based routing, and a visual check before a case is closed.

Smart reporting has three steps. The citizen signs in. The camera captures the problem together with the GPS position. The complaint is submitted with that location and time attached, so the report is tied to a real place.

The detection pipeline takes the photo, processes the scene, and labels what it finds. The example on this slide marks a pothole and a high severity. The same step can flag a second report that shows the same damage inside the same GPS area. A label is stored only when the configured vision model returns one.

Geographic intelligence tests the reported coordinates against stored administrative boundaries. The callout on this slide is an example match: Ward 4, Gram Panchayat. In the product, a jurisdiction is assigned only when a verified polygon contains the point. Otherwise the report stays pending verification.

Routing follows the issue and the matched boundary. A village road or local sanitation issue is sent to the Gram Panchayat. Block-level infrastructure goes to the Taluk Panchayat. A district highway or major utility goes to the Zilla Panchayat. Those routes come from rules an administrator has recorded. They are not guessed.

The official command dashboard is the desk for that authority. It shows where cases cluster, how many are new, pending, or resolved, and which ones need attention first. An official sees only the jurisdiction assigned to that account.

The workflow on this slide runs from reported, to analysis, to authority assigned, then work initiated, repair completed, verification, and closed. The citizen gets an in-app update when the case is routed, and another when it is resolved and verified.

Proof of work compares the original photo with the photo taken after the repair. The baseline shows the broken asset. The later photo is checked against it, so a case is not closed on a written claim alone.

The architecture has five layers. The React app sends the photo and the coordinates. FastAPI receives the report. Python runs the vision step when a model file is configured. The database answers the boundary query. The service is then hosted for the citizen and the official.

The stack on this slide is React, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Python, FastAPI, YOLO, OpenCV, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, and a maps API. Model training uses open road-damage datasets plus locally annotated photos. Detection in the app runs after those weights are supplied.

Security has three parts. Officials sign in, and each desk is limited to its own role and jurisdiction. Citizen photos stay on that account. GPS is saved only when the browser allows it. If location is denied, the photo is kept and the location is marked unavailable.

The roadmap separates the core from later work. The core is reporting, detection when the model is present, and routing from verified boundaries. Proposed later phases are a fuller government dashboard, stronger before-and-after checks, and maintenance forecasts from stored history.

NEXUS AI connects the citizen, the analysis, and the local authority. This closing slide names the outcome: faster routing, less manual overhead, transparent tracking, and planning based on the reports that were actually stored.
